Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: The assault happened at 3:15 p.m., exactly when the late afternoon sun hit the loading dock of the commercial building where Kai Tanuivi was finishing his electrical shift. He had just stepped outside to take a client call when the heavy steel door behind him slammed shut. Before he could turn, two men dragged him into the alley. The blows blurred into disjointed images of shins, gloves, and a glinting knife that remained fixed in Kai's mind like polaroids. When the attackers fled, Kai stood over his scattered tools, feeling completely detached, as though watching himself through thick glass. In the months that followed, that specific clock time and the sharp report of closing doors became unavoidable alarms. Whenever the clock on his work truck clicked past 3:15, or a garage door rattled open at a job site, Kai's body flooded with danger signals before his mind could catch up, causing him to flinch at a coworker's sudden movement or jump back when his girlfriend reached to steady him. Those sensory shocks would instantly pull those fragmented alley moments back into his head, and the sudden noise or time of day only reinforced his quiet conviction that he was fundamentally weak, a man who let his guard down while stronger individuals would never have been targeted. That quiet judgment of his own character only sharpened the danger signals, making him anticipate threats more acutely. Believing himself inherently flawed, he recalled the assault not as a chaotic struggle but as a series of frozen frames, each one burning with intense guilt and the crushing sense that the rest of the event was missing from his grasp. His self-blame made the 3:15 clock and the slamming doors feel even more invasive, as if time itself and the metal sounds were now personal indictments that could not be ignored. The sensory alarms of 3:15 and slamming doors directly pushed Kai toward escape, leading him to retreat to his truck and scroll endlessly through games or turn to alcohol. When the guilt-laden memories surfaced, Kai immediately reached for his phone or a bottle to dull the spike of panic. The return of those frozen memories reliably reignited his danger response, causing his body to brace against imagined attacks. Because the fear felt so immediate and unmanageable, Kai learned to numb it, turning to screens and alcohol to dampen the spike of dread. The shame of remembering only made the 3:15 clock and the garage doors feel more urgent, as if the past were actively hunting him in the present. Because the escape routines provided only temporary relief, Kai quickly convinced himself he was broken beyond repair and that his life had permanently derailed into a dead end. The more he isolated behind the blue glow of his phone and the bottle, the more the heavy doors and the ticking clock seemed to intrude on him, as if the avoidance itself had left him unprepared. Every missed diagnostic check where he chose a drink over conversation heightened his baseline anxiety, making his body jump at the slightest movement or touch, which only proved to him that his character was fatally flawed. He stopped watching crime dramas or reading true-crime books altogether, knowing the media would only act as a mirror to his terror. The cycle tightened as the months passed; he started avoiding his own neighborhood after the allotted time, taking circuitous routes home to dodge the familiar alley, while his foreman pulled him aside to question his reliability on complex commercial jobs. His girlfriend noticed the quiet distance, how he chose numbness over intimacy, but the fear of the clock and the sound made every shared moment feel like walking on thin ice. Now, sitting in the quiet intake room, Kai finally admitted he had reached the edge of his tether. He was terrified of what would happen if the memories stopped hiding behind his routines, and he hoped, desperately, to stop running from a time of day and a sound that had stolen his future.
